blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A factor stores each value together with its levels: the list of allowed categories, in a set order.

factor(x, levels = ...) makes a factor with the levels given. A value of x that is not among the levels becomes NA, without an error. With no levels given, they are taken from the data in alphabetical order.

Three functions come from the forcats package. The first, fct_recode(), renames levels, written new = "old", and leaves the others as they are. The second, fct_relevel(), moves the named levels to the front, written fct_relevel(x, "level"). The third, fct_infreq(), orders the levels by how many rows have each one, largest first. Each also takes a text column, and makes it a factor first, with its levels in alphabetical order.

count(), from dplyr, gives the number of rows for each value of one column, or for each combination of values of two or more columns. For a factor, .drop = FALSE also lists the combinations that never occur, with a count of 0.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
“Male”, “male” with a space at the end, and “M” are three different values to R.

count() shows you every value a column actually holds, and how many rows hold it. A misspelling shows up as an extra row.

Here is the trap. When you make a factor and a value is not on your list, R turns it into NA and says nothing.

Codes need the same care. A file may store sex as 1 and 2. Never guess the codes from the data.

Two counts at once, count(species, island), is Book 0’s two-way table, written as one row per pair.

blocks.label: Illustration 1
blocks.html:
Start with a column typed by hand. Here is a made-up register of six patients, with sex as the staff wrote it.

library(dplyr)
library(stringr)
library(forcats)

register <- tibble(
  id = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6),
  sex = c("Male", "male ", "Female", "F", "female", "MALE")
)

Attaching package: ‘dplyr’

The following objects are masked from ‘package:stats’:

    filter, lag

The following objects are masked from ‘package:base’:

    intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

You want two categories, female and male. Make a factor with those two levels, and count it:

register |>
  mutate(sex_f = factor(sex, levels = c("female", "male"))) |>
  count(sex_f)
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  sex_f      n
  <fct>  <int>
1 female     1
2 <NA>       5

One female, no male, and five missing. Not one value was missing in the register. factor() turned every value that did not match a level exactly into NA, and it gave no warning. A report built on this would say five patients’ sex was “not recorded”.

Go back a step and count the text as it is:

register |>
  count(sex)
# A tibble: 6 × 2
  sex          n
  <chr>    <int>
1 "F"          1
2 "Female"     1
3 "MALE"       1
4 "Male"       1
5 "female"     1
6 "male "      1

Six rows, six spellings, each held once. This is the count to run first, on every category column.

Now clean it in steps, each into a new column. Trim the spaces and lower the case, as the section on making new columns did. Then rename the one code that is left, “f”, with fct_recode(): the new name on the left, the old one on the right.

register <- register |>
  mutate(
    sex_clean = str_to_lower(str_trim(sex)),
    sex_f = fct_recode(sex_clean, female = "f"),
    sex_f = factor(sex_f, levels = c("female", "male"))
  )

register |>
  count(sex_f)
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  sex_f      n
  <fct>  <int>
1 female     3
2 male       3

Three female and three male, and no NA. The last line sets the order of the levels, so female comes first in every count and table, whatever order the data arrive in.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The six patients are made up. The spellings are the kind that hand entry produces; Broman and Woo’s advice on data entry warns against exactly this mix of “male” and ” male “.

Lowering the case and trimming spaces catches only these slips. “Mle” or “fem” would survive both steps, and the final factor() would turn them into NA. The count after the factor is what catches them, so never skip it.

blocks.label: Illustration 2
blocks.html:
Now codes. Many forms store a category as a number. Here is a made-up thesis dataset of five students, where sex is stored as 1 or 2. The data dictionary for this made-up study says 1 means female and 2 means male.

library(dplyr)
library(forcats)

students <- tibble(
  id = c(101, 102, 103, 104, 105),
  sex_code = c(1, 2, 2, 1, 2)
)

mean(students$sex_code)
[1] 1.6

R gives a mean sex of 1.6. The arithmetic is right and the number means nothing: 1 and 2 are labels, not amounts. A numeric code invites exactly this kind of summary.

Turn the code into a factor with the dictionary’s labels. fct_recode() works on text, so turn the numbers into text first with as.character(). Keep the code column beside the new one.

students <- students |>
  mutate(
    sex = fct_recode(as.character(sex_code), female = "1", male = "2")
  )

students

students |>
  count(sex)
# A tibble: 5 × 3
     id sex_code sex
  <dbl>    <dbl> <fct>
1   101        1 female
2   102        2 male
3   103        2 male
4   104        1 female
5   105        2 male
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  sex        n
  <fct>  <int>
1 female     2
2 male       3

Two female, three male. The column type now reads <fct>, a factor. Every label came from the dictionary, written once in the script, where anyone can check it against the dictionary.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html: The codes and their meanings are made up for this example. Another study may use 1 for male, or 0 and 1, or M and F. The labels in your script must come from your own data dictionary, never from this page or from habit.

blocks.label: Illustration 3
blocks.html:
Last, the penguin file. It has three category columns you will use often: species, island and sex. Count the islands first.

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(forcats)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

penguins_raw |>
  count(Island)
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  Island        n
  <chr>     <int>
1 Biscoe      168
2 Dream       124
3 Torgersen    52

The column is text, <chr>, so count() lists the islands alphabetically. A factor is something you choose to make.

Make the factors. Shorten the species names with fct_recode(), and order the islands by how many rows each has with fct_infreq().

penguins <- penguins_raw |>
  mutate(
    species = fct_recode(
      Species,
      Adelie = "Adelie Penguin (Pygoscelis adeliae)",
      Chinstrap = "Chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarctica)",
      Gentoo = "Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua)"
    ),
    island = fct_infreq(Island)
  )

levels(penguins$island)

penguins |>
  count(island)
[1] "Biscoe"    "Dream"     "Torgersen"
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  island        n
  <fct>     <int>
1 Biscoe      168
2 Dream       124
3 Torgersen    52

levels() lists a factor’s levels in their order. Biscoe comes first now, because it has the most rows. The counts are the same; only the order changed.

Island Rows
Biscoe 168
Dream 124
Torgersen 52

Now two columns at once. count(species, island) gives one row for each pair that occurs. With .drop = FALSE, it also gives the pairs that never occur, with 0:

penguins |>
  count(species, island, .drop = FALSE)
# A tibble: 9 × 3
  species   island        n
  <fct>     <fct>     <int>
1 Adelie    Biscoe       44
2 Adelie    Dream        56
3 Adelie    Torgersen    52
4 Chinstrap Biscoe        0
5 Chinstrap Dream        68
6 Chinstrap Torgersen     0
7 Gentoo    Biscoe      124
8 Gentoo    Dream         0
9 Gentoo    Torgersen     0

Nine rows: three species times three islands. Laid out as Book 0’s two-way table, with species down the side and islands across the top, the same counts read:

Species Biscoe Dream Torgersen
Adelie 44 56 52
Chinstrap 0 68 0
Gentoo 124 0 0

The zeros carry information. In this file, Chinstrap penguins were recorded only on Dream, and Gentoo only on Biscoe. Without .drop = FALSE, those zeros would not appear at all, and you might not notice that they exist.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The counts are rows of the file, which are nesting observations on the islands sampled. A zero says no such row was recorded. It does not say that no Chinstrap penguin lives on Biscoe.

fct_infreq() orders by the counts in this file. Another season’s file could order the islands differently, which matters if a report compares tables across files. A fixed order from fct_relevel() or from the levels you list yourself does not move.

points.html: Run count() on every category column before you use it.
factor() does not warn when a value matches no level. Count the factor after making it, and treat any new NA as a spelling you missed.
Refuse a summary that averages a code.
If you misspell an old level in fct_recode(), R warns “Unknown levels” and leaves that level unchanged.
Set the order of the levels on purpose, with the levels you list or with fct_relevel().
A table that leaves out its zeros hides that a combination never occurred.
A clean count shows how many rows hold each category. It cannot show that the category was recorded correctly in the first place.

blocks.prompt: In your penguin script, make sex a factor with the levels “female” and “male”, in that order, from the file’s Sex column. Count it, and say how many rows have no recorded sex.
blocks.answer:
library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(stringr)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

penguins <- penguins_raw |>
  mutate(sex = factor(str_to_lower(Sex), levels = c("female", "male")))

penguins |>
  count(sex)
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  sex        n
  <fct>  <int>
1 female   165
2 male     168
3 <NA>      11

165 female, 168 male, and 11 with no recorded sex. The file writes FEMALE and MALE in capitals, so the values are lowered first. Without str_to_lower(), factor() would match nothing, and all 344 rows would become NA. The 11 NAs here were already missing in the file, as the section on missing values counted.

blocks.prompt: Without looking back, say what factor() does with a value that is not among the levels you gave it. Then name the line you run to catch that.
blocks.answer: It turns the value into NA, with no warning. Catch it by running count() on the new factor and looking for an NA row that was not there before.

blocks.prompt: A first-year resident has ten minutes and a whiteboard. Their thesis data has a column tobacco coded 0, 1 and 2, and they have reported “mean tobacco use 0.8”. Explain what is wrong, and show them how to fix it.
blocks.answer:
Write the three codes on the board and ask what each means. They will have to look in the data dictionary, which is the point. The numbers are labels, and only the dictionary says what they stand for. Suppose it says 0 never, 1 former, 2 current.

Ask what “0.8” means. It is not a kind of tobacco use. It is an average of labels, like averaging bed numbers. A different coding, 1 to 3 instead of 0 to 2, would give a different “mean” for the same people.

Then write the fix. Turn the code into a factor with the dictionary’s labels: fct_recode(as.character(tobacco), never = "0", former = "1", current = "2"). Keep the code column beside it. Report a count of each category with its share, not a mean.

blocks.prompt:
Before you run it, say in what order the levels come.

factor(c("Dream", "Biscoe", "Dream", "Torgersen"))
blocks.answer:
factor(c("Dream", "Biscoe", "Dream", "Torgersen"))
[1] Dream     Biscoe    Dream     Torgersen
Levels: Biscoe Dream Torgersen

The levels are Biscoe, Dream, Torgersen: with no levels given, factor() takes them from the data in alphabetical order.

blocks.prompt:
Before you run it, say what the levels of the result are, in order.

library(forcats)

fct_infreq(c("rice", "roti", "rice", "millet", "rice", "roti"))
blocks.answer:
library(forcats)

fct_infreq(c("rice", "roti", "rice", "millet", "rice", "roti"))
[1] rice   roti   rice   millet rice   roti
Levels: rice roti millet

rice, roti, millet. Rice appears three times, roti twice and millet once, and fct_infreq() puts the most frequent first. The values themselves do not move.

blocks.prompt:
A made-up column codes the meal eaten as 1 (breakfast), 2 (lunch) or 3 (dinner). Turn it into a factor with those labels.

meal_code <- c(2, 3, 3, 1, 2)
blocks.answer:
library(forcats)

fct_recode(as.character(meal_code), breakfast = "1", lunch = "2", dinner = "3")
[1] lunch     dinner    dinner    breakfast lunch
Levels: breakfast lunch dinner

lunch, dinner, dinner, breakfast, lunch. fct_recode() takes text, so the numbers are turned into text first. Each new label sits on the left of its old code.

blocks.prompt:
Read the penguin file.

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

Count the rows for each value of Clutch Completion. What does a “No” mean, according to the data’s help page?
blocks.answer:
penguins_raw |>
  count(`Clutch Completion`)
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  `Clutch Completion`     n
  <chr>               <int>
1 No                     36
2 Yes                   308

36 rows say “No” and 308 say “Yes”, which add to 344. The help page describes the column as whether the study nest was “observed with a full clutch, i.e., 2 eggs”. So “No” means the nest was not seen with two eggs.

blocks.prompt:
Read the penguin file.

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(forcats)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

Make a factor of island in which Torgersen comes first and the other islands keep their alphabetical order. Count it.
blocks.answer:
penguins_raw |>
  mutate(island = fct_relevel(Island, "Torgersen")) |>
  count(island)
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  island        n
  <fct>     <int>
1 Torgersen    52
2 Biscoe      168
3 Dream       124

Torgersen 52, Biscoe 168, Dream 124. fct_relevel() moves the named level to the front. It leaves the rest in their existing order, which for a text column is alphabetical.

blocks.prompt:
A colleague makes a factor from a made-up register and reports: “2 of the 6 patients were female.”

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

register <- tibble(sex = c("female", "Female", "male", "female", "Female ", "male"))

register |>
  mutate(sex = factor(sex, levels = c("female", "male"))) |>
  count(sex)
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  sex        n
  <fct>  <int>
1 female     2
2 male       2
3 <NA>       2

Find what broke, and why the report looks reasonable.
blocks.answer:
Two “Female” values have a capital letter, and one also has a space at the end. Neither matches the level “female”, so factor() turned both into NA without a warning. Two females became missing, and the colleague read only the female row.

Clean the text first:

library(stringr)

register |>
  mutate(sex = factor(str_to_lower(str_trim(sex)), levels = c("female", "male"))) |>
  count(sex)
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  sex        n
  <fct>  <int>
1 female     4
2 male       2

4 of the 6 were female.

Why the wrong report looks reasonable: the count printed a female row and a male row, the two categories that were expected. The NA row was below them, and nobody asked why a register with no gaps had two missing values.

blocks.prompt:
A colleague shortens the species names in the penguin file:

library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(forcats)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

penguins_raw |>
  mutate(
    species = fct_recode(
      Species,
      Adelie = "Adelie Penguin (Pygoscelis adeliae)",
      Chinstrap = "Chinstrap Penguin (Pygoscelis antarctica)",
      Gentoo = "Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua)"
    )
  ) |>
  count(species)
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  species                                       n
  <fct>                                     <int>
1 Adelie                                      152
2 Chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarctica)    68
3 Gentoo                                      124
Warning message:
There was 1 warning in `mutate()`.
ℹ In argument: `species = fct_recode(...)`.
Caused by warning:
! Unknown levels in `f`: Chinstrap Penguin (Pygoscelis antarctica)

Their table has three rows, labelled “Adelie”, “Chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarctica)” and “Gentoo”. They decide the file’s Chinstrap name is “too long to fix” and leave it. Find what broke.
blocks.answer:
The old name for Chinstrap was typed with a capital P, “Penguin”. The file writes “penguin”. The name did not match, so fct_recode() warned “Unknown levels” and left the level as it was. The warning said what happened.

Copy the old names from a count() of the column, not from memory:

penguins_raw |>
  mutate(
    species = fct_recode(
      Species,
      Adelie = "Adelie Penguin (Pygoscelis adeliae)",
      Chinstrap = "Chinstrap penguin (Pygoscelis antarctica)",
      Gentoo = "Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua)"
    )
  ) |>
  count(species)
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  species       n
  <fct>     <int>
1 Adelie      152
2 Chinstrap    68
3 Gentoo      124

Adelie 152, Chinstrap 68, Gentoo 124.

Why the wrong conclusion looks reasonable: the counts were right and only a label was long, so it looked like a cosmetic problem. It was a typing error that the warning had already named.

blocks.prompt:
A made-up study’s data dictionary says sex is coded 1 = male, 2 = female. A resident writes:

library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(forcats)

study <- tibble(sex_code = c(2, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2))

study |>
  mutate(sex = fct_recode(as.character(sex_code), female = "1", male = "2")) |>
  count(sex)
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  sex        n
  <fct>  <int>
1 female     2
2 male       5

Their results say “5 of the 7 participants were male”. Find what broke.
blocks.answer:
The labels are swapped. The dictionary says 1 is male, and the code says 1 is female. Every participant has the wrong label, and the code ran without a warning, because R has no way to know what the codes mean.

study |>
  mutate(sex = fct_recode(as.character(sex_code), male = "1", female = "2")) |>
  count(sex)
# A tibble: 2 × 2
  sex        n
  <fct>  <int>
1 male       2
2 female     5

5 of the 7 were female and 2 were male.

Why the wrong answer looks reasonable: the code is tidy and the counts add up. A swap of labels changes no total. Only a line-by-line check against the dictionary catches it, so copy the labels from the dictionary into a comment beside the line.

blocks.prompt: A made-up draft report says: “Of the 333 penguins with sex recorded, 168 were male.” Check the sentence against the penguin file and say what it does not establish.
blocks.answer:
library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

penguins_raw |>
  count(Sex)
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  Sex        n
  <chr>  <int>
1 FEMALE   165
2 MALE     168
3 <NA>      11

168 MALE and 165 FEMALE make 333 with sex recorded, and 11 more have none. The sentence matches the file’s rows. 168 of 333 is 50.5 per cent.

What it does not establish:

  • That the colony is about half male. The rows are nesting observations of birds that were sampled, not a count of every penguin.
  • Anything about the birds in the 11 rows with no recorded sex.
  • That each row is a different bird. The file’s IDs repeat, as an earlier section showed.

blocks.prompt: In a made-up meeting, someone says: “The penguin data show that Gentoo penguins live only on Biscoe.” Turn the claim into a count, run it, and say what the result does and does not establish.
blocks.answer:
library(readr)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
library(forcats)

penguins_raw <- read_csv(
  here::here("data-raw", "penguins_raw.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

penguins_raw |>
  mutate(island = factor(Island)) |>
  filter(Species == "Gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua)") |>
  count(island, .drop = FALSE)
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  island        n
  <fct>     <int>
1 Biscoe      124
2 Dream         0
3 Torgersen     0

All 124 Gentoo rows are from Biscoe, with 0 from Dream and 0 from Torgersen. Making the island a factor first, with .drop = FALSE, keeps the zeros in view.

What it establishes: in this file, every Gentoo row was recorded on Biscoe.

What it does not establish:

  • Where Gentoo penguins live. The file covers three islands near one research station, and only the nests the study chose to sample. A zero means none was recorded, not none exists.
  • Why. Whether the study went looking for Gentoo on Dream and Torgersen, the file does not say.
  • The claim in the meeting moved from “were recorded only on” to “live only on”. That move is the error.
